title: Frontend Programming
description: Learn how browsers turn HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into usable interfaces, then build and publish a small web app.

paths.title: Web Foundations
paths.description: Understand the browser, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, events, and semantics.

paths.title: Build Your First Web App
paths.description: Create, test, and publish a small interactive browser application.

paths.title: Modern Frontend Essentials
paths.description: Study components, responsiveness, accessibility, APIs, and quality checks.

cards.title: What the frontend is
cards.prompt: The frontend is the part of an application that people directly see and interact with.
cards.content: A frontend includes the page structure, visual styling, buttons, forms, navigation, animations, and the browser-side logic that responds to users. It usually runs in a web browser.

cards.title: The browser reads three core languages
cards.prompt: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript have different jobs, but they work together to create a web page.
cards.content: HTML gives the page structure and meaning. CSS controls appearance and layout. JavaScript adds behavior, data handling, and interaction.

cards.title: HTML describes meaning
cards.prompt: Good HTML does more than put text on a screen; it describes what each part of the page represents.
cards.content: Semantic elements such as <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <button> help browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies understand the page.

cards.title: Choose the correct HTML element
cards.prompt: Which element should normally trigger an action such as opening a menu?

question.explanation: A button is keyboard-accessible by default and communicates that it performs an action.

cards.title: CSS controls presentation
cards.prompt: CSS selects HTML elements and applies visual rules to them.
cards.content: A CSS rule has a selector and one or more declarations. The browser combines many rules through the cascade, inheritance, and selector specificity.

cards.title: A basic CSS rule
cards.prompt: This rule styles every primary button that uses the class name shown below.
cards.content: The selector targets elements with class="primary-button". The declarations set the text color, background, spacing, and rounded corners.

cards.title: JavaScript responds to events
cards.prompt: An event is something that happens in the browser, such as a click, key press, form submission, or completed network request.
cards.content: JavaScript can listen for an event and run a function in response. This is the foundation of interactive interfaces.

cards.title: Separate structure from behavior
cards.prompt: Which language is primarily responsible for changing page behavior after a user clicks a button?

question.explanation: JavaScript runs browser-side logic and can update the document after events.

cards.title: Create your first web app folder
cards.prompt: Start with a small, predictable project structure before writing features.
cards.content: Keeping files separated makes the project easier to understand and expand.
steps: Create a new folder named my-first-web-app.
Open the folder in your code editor.

cards.title: Build the page structure
cards.prompt: The first version needs a heading, a short instruction, a button, and a result area.
cards.content: The script is loaded with defer so it runs after the HTML has been parsed. The output paragraph includes an id so JavaScript can find it.

code.snippet:
Daily Greeting

Press the button to create a greeting.

cards.title: Add simple visual styling
cards.prompt: Use CSS to make the first app readable without depending on a framework.
cards.content: The layout centers a card on the page, limits line length, and gives the button a clear interactive appearance.

cards.title: Connect the button to JavaScript
cards.prompt: Select the page elements, listen for a click, and update the output.
cards.content: querySelector finds elements in the document. addEventListener connects the click to a function. textContent safely replaces the visible text.

cards.title: Test the first app
cards.prompt: A feature is not finished until its basic behavior and failure cases have been checked.
cards.content: Use the browser developer tools when something does not work. The Console often reveals spelling errors, missing files, or invalid JavaScript.
items: The page loads without a blank screen.
The CSS file changes the appearance.
The button can be reached with the Tab key.
Pressing Enter or Space activates the button.
The greeting appears after a click.
The browser Console shows no errors.

cards.title: The DOM is the page as objects
cards.prompt: The Document Object Model, or DOM, represents HTML elements as objects JavaScript can read and change.
cards.content: When JavaScript updates text, attributes, classes, or elements, it is usually changing the DOM. The browser then redraws the affected interface.

cards.title: Find an element by id
cards.prompt: Which expression selects the element whose HTML id is output?

question.explanation: In a CSS selector, # identifies an id. querySelector accepts CSS selector syntax.

cards.title: State is information that can change
cards.prompt: Interface state is the current information that determines what the user sees.
cards.content: Examples include the selected tab, whether a menu is open, form values, loading status, and fetched data. As apps grow, keeping state predictable becomes important.

cards.title: Store a small piece of state
cards.prompt: A counter shows the cycle: read state, update state, then render the new value.
cards.content: The count variable stores state. Every click updates the value and writes the current state into the page.

cards.title: Publish a static web app
cards.prompt: A plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript app can be deployed as static files.
cards.content: Static hosting is suitable when the browser can perform all required work and no secret server credentials are needed.
items: Keep index.html at the project root.
Commit the project to a Git repository.
Choose a static host such as GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, or Vercel.
Open the deployed URL on both mobile and desktop.
Check the Console and Network panels for missing files.

cards.title: Components divide an interface
cards.prompt: A component is a reusable, self-contained part of an interface with a clear responsibility.
cards.content: A navigation bar, card, modal, search field, and data table can each become a component. Component boundaries make large interfaces easier to reason about.

cards.title: Responsive design adapts to available space
cards.prompt: Responsive interfaces change layout and sizing rather than assuming one screen width.
cards.content: Useful tools include flexible units, min/max constraints, CSS Grid, Flexbox, container queries, and media queries. Start with a usable small-screen layout, then enhance it.

cards.title: Protect accessibility semantics
cards.prompt: Which approach is usually best for a clickable control?

options: A div with an onclick handler
A span with a pointer cursor
A native button with a clear label
An image with no alternative text
question.explanation: Native controls provide keyboard behavior, focus handling, and semantics without recreating them manually.

cards.title: Frontend apps consume APIs
cards.prompt: An API gives the frontend a structured way to request or send data.
cards.content: The browser commonly sends HTTP requests and receives JSON. The interface must handle loading, success, empty, and error states instead of assuming every request succeeds.

cards.title: Fetch data safely
cards.prompt: A basic request should check the HTTP response before using its data.
cards.content: fetch resolves for many HTTP errors, so checking response.ok prevents a 404 or 500 response from being treated as success. try/catch handles network and parsing failures.

cards.title: Frontend quality baseline
cards.prompt: Use this checklist before calling a frontend feature complete.
cards.content: Quality is a combination of correct behavior, understandable code, inclusive interaction, performance, and clear failure handling.
items: The feature works with keyboard input.
Labels and headings clearly describe the interface.
Loading, empty, success, and error states are visible.
The layout works at narrow and wide widths.
User input is validated and escaped where needed.
The browser Console has no unexpected errors.
